quest.oneLiner: Requirements gathering is writing down what a system must do, how well it must do it, and how you will check it.

story.pain: Teams started building features without clear goals, causing missed deadlines, cost overruns, and AI agents that gave wrong answers.
story.idea: Write functional and non‑functional requirements up front and add a metric for acceptable AI accuracy before any code is written.
story.unlocked: The team can build the FoodieGo support agent with known limits and measurable success criteria.
story.origin: Requirements gathering is defined as the process of generating a list of functional and non‑functional requirements from stakeholders [4].

beforeAfter.how: Developers discuss ideas on a whiteboard and start coding immediately.
beforeAfter.breaks: Leads to vague scope, hidden assumptions, and hard‑to‑measure outcomes.

beforeAfter.how: Product owners write user stories and the team estimates effort in story points.
beforeAfter.breaks: Stories often miss performance or cost constraints, and AI‑specific accuracy is not captured.

beforeAfter.approach: Formal requirements gathering with AI accuracy clause
beforeAfter.how: Define functional requirements (e.g., answer order status, process refunds), non‑functional requirements (reply < 3 s, cost < ₹0.50 per chat, 80 % self‑resolution), and an accuracy threshold for the AI agent.
beforeAfter.breaks: Requires disciplined documentation and agreement but provides a clear testable target.

production.title: Validate order status query
production.text: FoodieGo's AI must return the correct order status within 3 seconds for 95 % of queries; test harness checks latency and compares answer to the order database [4].

production.title: Cost‑per‑chat monitoring
production.text: Instrument the chat service to log token usage; ensure average cost stays below ₹0.50 per interaction, alerting if the model drift raises cost [6].

production.title: Self‑resolution rate report
production.text: Measure the percentage of chats closed without human hand‑off; aim for ≥ 80 % as defined in the non‑functional requirements [4].

qa: Write test cases that verify functional and non‑functional requirements.
Create scripts to measure latency and cost per chat.
frontend: Display error messages when the AI fails the accuracy threshold.
Show latency indicators to the user.
backend: Implement logging for cost and performance metrics.
Expose an endpoint for automated requirement validation.
leadership: Approve the accuracy and cost thresholds before release.
Track requirement compliance in product dashboards.

items.what: Generates draft requirements from stakeholder interviews [6]

items.name: Collaborative wiki
items.what: Stores functional and non‑functional specs for all teams

items.name: Latency tester
items.what: Measures response time of the FoodieGo agent

items.name: Cost calculator
items.what: Converts token usage to monetary cost

items.name: Accuracy evaluator
items.what: Runs a held‑out set of queries to compute AI correctness

atScale.lead: Prototyping a requirement list is easy; keeping the AI within those limits for millions of users is the real work.

ops.name: Monitoring
ops.text: Continuous tracking of latency, cost, and accuracy in production.

ops.name: Alerting
ops.text: Automatic alerts when any metric breaches its threshold.

ops.name: Retraining
ops.text: Periodic model updates to maintain the required accuracy.

ops.name: Governance
ops.text: Review and adjust requirements as business goals evolve.

atScale.takeaway: The model is only a fraction of the effort; most work is in defining, measuring, and enforcing the requirements.

quest.oneLiner: A Stateless LLM API is like a REST endpoint: each call carries the whole conversation and the model forgets everything after responding.

story.pain: Developers had to store chat state inside the model, causing leaks, scaling limits, and privacy risks.
story.idea: Make the API stateless and let the backend keep the full message list and send it every time.
story.unlocked: Now you can scale horizontally, audit logs, and control context precisely.
story.origin: Statelessness of LLMs is described in multiple sources, e.g., the model discards all computation after each call [2] and the REST‑style API model is explained in an AI model guide [8].

beforeAfter.how: The LLM service keeps a session ID and stores prior messages on the provider side.
beforeAfter.breaks: Limits parallelism, can mix user data, and makes privacy compliance hard [3][1].

beforeAfter.how: The front‑end bundles recent messages in a cookie or local storage and sends only new tokens.
beforeAfter.breaks: Runs into token limits quickly, forces frequent truncation, and loses control over what the model sees [5].

beforeAfter.how: Each request contains a full "messages" array. The backend trims or summarizes to fit the model's context window and pays per token each time.
beforeAfter.breaks: Costs rise with conversation length because every turn repeats earlier tokens [1][5].

production.title: FoodieGo order help
production.text: When a user asks, "Where is my order?", the backend adds the new query to the full chat history, trims to the last 4 k tokens, and calls the LLM. The model replies with a personalized status update. This works at scale because each call is independent [2][8].

production.title: Menu recommendation
production.text: FoodieGo asks the model to suggest dishes based on prior user preferences. The backend builds a context that includes the user's past likes, summarises older likes, and sends the whole array. The stateless call returns a ranked list without any hidden state on the model side [4].

production.title: Support ticket triage
production.text: Support agents submit a ticket text. The backend prepends the latest ticket and a short system prompt, then calls the LLM to classify urgency. Because the API is stateless, the classification logic lives entirely in the service, ensuring auditability and privacy [3].

qa: Verify that the message array respects the token limit.
Check that truncation does not drop required context.
frontend: Collect user input and send it as a new entry in the messages list.
Show token usage to avoid surprise costs.
backend: Store full conversation history in a database.
Summarize or prune old messages to fit the model's context window.
leadership: Track per‑message cost and set budget alerts.
Define policies for how long conversation history is retained.

items.what: Store message history and enable vector search for retrieval‑augmented context.

items.what: Load‑test the stateless endpoint to verify horizontal scaling.

items.name: OpenAI compatible LLM API
items.what: Provides the stateless inference endpoint that reads the messages array.

items.name: Auth0
items.what: Manages API keys and rate‑limit per client.

atScale.lead: A demo can be built in a day, but production requires robust history storage, token budgeting, and observability.

ops.name: Cost
ops.text: Token count grows with conversation length; need monitoring.

ops.name: Freshness
ops.text: Backend must keep the latest data (e.g., order status) in the context.

ops.name: Observability
ops.text: Log request/response pairs for debugging and compliance.

atScale.takeaway: Most of the work is engineering the surrounding system—storage, trimming, security, and cost control.

quest.oneLiner: A system prompt is a fixed set of instructions written by developers that tells the model how to act before any user query arrives.

story.pain: Early chatbots answered anything in a generic way, often giving the wrong tone or revealing internal logic, and they were vulnerable to prompt injection.
story.idea: Add a developer‑controlled system prompt that defines role, tone, scope, and hard rules for every conversation.
story.unlocked: The AI can now stay on brand, follow safety rules, and handle edge cases reliably, making it suitable for production support.
story.origin: System prompts were described as the instructional layer of LLMs in the AI Context Engineering Bootcamp [3] and highlighted as essential for production AI apps by multiple guides [4][6][7].

beforeAfter.how: Send only the user query to the model and rely on its default behavior.
beforeAfter.breaks: Model may ignore needed constraints, give inconsistent tone, and be easy to hijack.

beforeAfter.how: Write if‑else logic around model outputs to enforce policies.
beforeAfter.breaks: Rules are brittle, hard to update, and cannot influence the model’s internal generation.

beforeAfter.how: Provide a fixed instruction block (role, tone, scope, hard rules) as part of every request.
beforeAfter.breaks: A clever user can still try to override it, and the prompt must be carefully crafted to avoid ambiguity.

production.title: Consistent brand voice
production.text: FoodieGo’s AI support agent always replies in a friendly, casual tone and mentions the company name, thanks to a system prompt that sets the role and tone [4][6].

production.title: Escalation handling
production.text: The system prompt instructs the agent to hand off to a human when it cannot answer a delivery question, reducing user frustration [8].

production.title: Prompt‑injection defense
production.text: Defensive instructions in the system prompt tell the model to ignore attempts to change its behavior, protecting the service from malicious inputs [4][8].

qa: Verify that the system prompt produces the expected tone in test conversations.
Check that edge‑case inputs do not bypass hard rules.
frontend: Display the agent’s messages knowing they follow the defined style.
Pass user text unchanged to the backend; do not add extra prompts.
backend: Store and version the system prompt alongside code.
Log model responses to monitor compliance with the prompt.
leadership: Allocate budget for prompt‑management tooling.
Set policy on prompt review cycles to keep tone and rules up to date.

items.what: Collaborative editing and validation of prompt files.

items.what: Inject the system prompt into every chain call automatically.

items.what: Build dynamic system prompts with conditionals.

items.name: OpenTelemetry
items.what: Track latency and error rates of prompt‑driven requests.

items.name: Prometheus
items.what: Alert on spikes that may indicate prompt‑injection attempts.

atScale.lead: A demo with a static system prompt is easy, but running it for millions of users requires robust prompt versioning, monitoring, and security.

ops.name: Prompt Design
ops.text: Write clear, specific role and rule statements.

ops.name: Versioning
ops.text: Track changes and roll back if a new prompt breaks behavior.

ops.name: Monitoring
ops.text: Collect metrics on compliance and injection attempts.

ops.name: Security
ops.text: Enforce immutable system prompts and sanitize user input.

ops.name: Latency
ops.text: Ensure the prompt size does not add noticeable delay.

ops.name: Scaling
ops.text: Cache the prompt with the model instance to avoid repeated loading.

atScale.takeaway: Most of the work is building the surrounding engineering around the prompt, not the model itself.

quest.oneLiner: Structured output forces the model to return data that matches a JSON schema, so your code can rely on the shape of the response.

story.pain: LLM replies are free‑form text. Teams spend time parsing, validating, and fixing broken formats, which adds bugs and cost.
story.idea: Define a JSON schema and let the model API enforce it; the model must emit valid JSON or it is rejected.
story.unlocked: Applications can consume model data directly without fragile post‑processing, enabling reliable agents like FoodieGo’s AI support.
story.origin: OpenAI and Google introduced schema‑enforced outputs to solve the unpredictability of free‑form replies [1][4][8].

beforeAfter.how: Run a regular expression on the model's raw text to extract fields.
beforeAfter.breaks: Regex is brittle, fails on any variation, and requires constant updates.

beforeAfter.how: Generate free text, then parse with a JSON parser and catch errors.
beforeAfter.breaks: Most calls fail validation, causing retries and latency spikes.

beforeAfter.how: Define a JSON schema in the request; the API only returns responses that conform.
beforeAfter.breaks: If the schema is too strict, the model may refuse to answer, so design schemas with reasonable defaults.

production.title: Order status lookup
production.text: FoodieGo’s assistant receives a user query and returns {orderId:string, status:string, eta:number} validated by the schema, letting the frontend render instantly [2][4].

production.title: Restaurant recommendation
production.text: The model returns a list of restaurant objects (name, cuisine, rating) that matches the schema, so the backend can store them without extra cleaning [1][7].

production.title: Support ticket triage
production.text: AI extracts ticket fields (category, priority, description) into a schema‑compliant JSON that feeds directly into the ticketing system, eliminating manual entry [6][9].

qa: Write schema‑based contract tests.
Verify that every API call returns valid JSON.
frontend: Consume the exact fields without defensive checks.
Display data instantly, trusting the shape.
backend: Define schemas once and reuse across services.
Log schema violations as alerts.
leadership: Allocate budget for schema design instead of ad‑hoc parsing tools.
Set reliability KPIs based on schema compliance.

items.what: Fast JSON schema validator used in Node services.

items.what: Python library that enforces schemas on incoming data.

atScale.lead: Demoing a schema‑enforced call is trivial; keeping it reliable for millions of users requires robust tooling and monitoring.

ops.name: Schema design
ops.text: Create and version JSON schemas for each model endpoint.

ops.name: Validation layer
ops.text: Add runtime validators to catch any non‑conforming responses.

ops.name: Monitoring
ops.text: Track schema violation rates and alert on spikes.

ops.name: Retry logic
ops.text: Gracefully fallback when the model rejects a request.

atScale.takeaway: Most of the work is engineering the contracts, validation, and observability, not the model itself.

quest.oneLiner: RAG lets an AI look up current documents at query time instead of memorising them.

story.pain: LLMs often answer from stale training data and can hallucinate, which broke trust in support bots.
story.idea: Combine the model with a searchable knowledge base: split docs, embed them, query the index for each user question, and feed the result to the model.
story.unlocked: Support agents can give up‑to‑date answers with source citations without retraining the model.
story.origin: The term Retrieval‑Augmented Generation was coined in a 2020 paper describing a hybrid of a parametric model and external memory [1][3].

beforeAfter.how: Train the LLM on a snapshot of policies so it can answer from memory.
beforeAfter.breaks: Every policy change requires costly retraining; the model still hallucinates on rare topics.

beforeAfter.how: Provide the model with example Q&A pairs in the prompt to steer answers.
beforeAfter.breaks: Prompt length is limited; examples become outdated quickly and cannot cover all policies.

beforeAfter.how: Chunk policy docs, embed chunks, store in a vector DB, retrieve relevant chunks per query, and generate an answer with citations.
beforeAfter.breaks: Requires building and maintaining the retrieval pipeline, but avoids retraining.

production.title: Customer support for FoodieGo
production.text: When a rider asks why a restaurant was cancelled, the AI pulls the latest cancellation policy from the internal docs and replies with a citation, keeping answers fresh without model updates [5][8].

production.title: Internal knowledge base
production.text: Engineers query the RAG bot for deployment guidelines; it retrieves the current CI/CD playbook and cites the exact section, reducing time spent searching [4][7].

production.title: Policy compliance checks
production.text: The bot checks a new promotion against the latest pricing rules by retrieving the rule set and confirming compliance, avoiding manual audits [2][9].

qa: Create test cases that verify citations match retrieved chunks.
Monitor hallucination rates before and after RAG rollout.
frontend: Display retrieved citations alongside answers.
Show a loading indicator while the retrieval step runs.
backend: Implement chunking, embedding, and vector store queries.
Add fallback to plain LLM if retrieval fails.
leadership: Track cost savings from not retraining models.
Set policy for how often docs are re‑ingested.

items.what: Generative model that consumes the retrieved context.

items.what: Creates vector representations of document chunks.

atScale.lead: A demo can be built in a day, but production needs a robust ingestion pipeline, monitoring, and security.

ops.name: Freshness
ops.text: Schedule regular re‑indexing of docs to keep citations current.

ops.name: Latency
ops.text: Cache frequent queries and optimise vector DB sharding.

ops.name: Security
ops.text: Encrypt stored embeddings and restrict query access.

ops.name: Observability
ops.text: Log retrieval scores and citation usage for debugging.

atScale.takeaway: Most effort is in data pipelines, storage, and ops; the model itself is just one component.

quest.oneLiner: Tool calling lets an LLM ask your code to run a specific function and then use the result.

story.pain: LLMs could only return text, so they could not fetch live data or perform actions like placing an order.
story.idea: Define a tool (name, description, input schema). The model decides when to call it, your code runs it, and the result is fed back.
story.unlocked: Agents can now book a restaurant, check order status, or query a database in real time.
story.origin: Tool calling grew from the ReAct pattern that combined reasoning and acting steps [1] and was later formalized as function calling in LLM APIs [3][4].

beforeAfter.how: Write prompts that ask the model to embed data in its answer, hoping it knows the latest info.
beforeAfter.breaks: Model knowledge is stale; no guaranteed access to real‑time data; brittle when data changes.

beforeAfter.how: Your service fetches data (e.g., from a DB) and appends it to the prompt before sending it to the model.
beforeAfter.breaks: Hard to keep context consistent; limited token budget; you must decide when to retrieve yourself.

beforeAfter.how: Define tools with JSON schemas. The model outputs a function call; your runtime executes it and returns the output as a new message.
beforeAfter.breaks: Requires orchestration, auth, and error handling, but gives reliable, typed interactions.

production.title: Order status lookup
production.text: User asks "Where is my pizza?". The model calls the `getOrderStatus` tool with order ID, your code queries the delivery service, and the result is shown to the user [2][4].

production.title: Menu recommendation
production.text: User says "I want a vegan meal near me". The model calls `searchRestaurants` with dietary filters, your service hits a geo‑API, and the model formats the top picks [2][6].

production.title: Support ticket escalation
production.text: User reports a bug. The model calls `createTicket` with details; your backend creates a ticket in the issue tracker and returns the ticket ID for confirmation [5][7].

qa: Write tests that verify the model produces correctly structured calls.
Validate error paths when a tool fails.
frontend: Display tool results as part of the chat UI.
Handle loading states while a tool runs.
backend: Implement the tool functions and secure their execution.
Log each call for monitoring and debugging.
leadership: Prioritize which business actions need a tool.
Allocate resources for the orchestration layer.

items.name: Tool schema
items.what: JSON definition of name, description, and input fields.

items.name: Executor
items.what: Code that parses the model's call, runs the function, and formats the output.

items.name: Gateway
items.what: API layer that routes calls, handles auth, and returns results to the model.

items.name: Monitoring
items.what: Track latency, errors, and usage of each tool.

atScale.lead: A demo can be built in a few hours, but production needs a full orchestration service.

ops.name: Auth
ops.text: Secure credential handling for each external API.

ops.name: Latency
ops.text: Measure and bound tool execution time to keep chat responsive.

ops.name: Error handling
ops.text: Gracefully recover from tool failures and return useful messages.

ops.name: Observability
ops.text: Log calls, monitor success rates, and alert on anomalies.

atScale.takeaway: The model is just the decision maker; most work is building a reliable, secure tool‑execution layer.

quest.oneLiner: MCP is a universal protocol that lets AI agents talk to tools and data sources the same way a USB cable lets devices connect.

story.pain: Before MCP each AI model needed a custom connector for every tool, creating an M × N explosion of code and maintenance.
story.idea: MCP defines a common JSON‑RPC‑based language and a server that wraps tools, so any model can call any tool through a single interface.
story.unlocked: Teams can add a new service once and instantly make it usable by all AI agents, reducing integration time and bugs.
story.origin: Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024 as an open standard to solve the M × N problem, inspired by the Language Server Protocol [1][4][5].

beforeAfter.how: Each model had its own SDK that directly invoked a specific API endpoint.
beforeAfter.breaks: Scaling requires writing a new wrapper for every model‑tool pair; security and versioning are fragmented.

beforeAfter.how: Teams built a thin service per tool that translated a model's request into the tool's API.
beforeAfter.breaks: Still M × N: every new model needs a new adapter for each tool, and discovery is manual.

beforeAfter.how: An MCP server implements a standard JSON‑RPC interface for a tool; an MCP client (the AI app) talks to any server using the same protocol.
beforeAfter.breaks: None listed; MCP reduces the integration matrix to M + N.

production.title: Customer‑support agent for FoodieGo
production.text: The AI agent asks the MCP server for the latest order status, then sends a confirmation email—all using the same MCP call pattern, eliminating separate webhook code [9][10].

production.title: Menu‑search RAG
production.text: FoodieGo exposes its restaurant catalog as an MCP tool; the agent retrieves relevant dishes in real time, improving answer accuracy without custom search integration [9][13].

production.title: Dynamic pricing workflow
production.text: A pricing microservice is wrapped by an MCP server; the AI can request a price quote and automatically apply discounts, keeping business logic centralized [9][15].

qa: Validate MCP request/response schemas with simple JSON tests.
Check that tool permissions are enforced by the MCP server.
frontend: Invoke MCP client methods from the UI when a user asks a question.
Show loading states based on MCP call latency.
backend: Implement MCP servers for each internal service (order, menu, pricing).
Maintain versioned tool manifests for safe upgrades.
leadership: Track integration velocity – new tool added = one MCP server, not many adapters.
Assess security posture via MCP audit logs.

items.name: MCP Server SDK
items.what: Library to expose any service as an MCP‑compatible tool (Python, Node, Go).

items.name: MCP Client Library
items.what: Runtime that lets an LLM send JSON‑RPC requests to any MCP server.

items.name: MCP Mock Server
items.what: Fake server that returns deterministic responses for unit tests.

items.name: Schema Validator
items.what: Tool that checks request and response payloads against the MCP JSON‑RPC schema.

items.name: Tool Registry
items.what: Central catalog of available MCP tools with version and permission metadata.

items.name: Discovery Proxy
items.what: Service that lets the AI ask “what tools are available?” and receives the registry list.

atScale.lead: Demoing MCP with one tool is easy; running dozens of secure, audited tool servers for millions of users is the real engineering effort.

ops.name: Security
ops.text: Enforce per‑tool auth, audit logs, and protect against tool‑poisoning attacks.

ops.name: Observability

ops.name: Scaling
ops.text: Load‑balance MCP servers, auto‑scale containers, and cache frequent tool responses.

quest.oneLiner: An agent loop is a repeatable cycle where an LLM thinks, uses a tool, watches the result, and decides whether to keep going.

story.pain: LLMs that answer once cannot finish long‑horizon tasks; they stop after a single call and leave work half‑done [2][7].
story.idea: The agent loop interleaves reasoning (think) with tool use (act) and observation, repeating until a stop condition is met [1][4].
story.unlocked: Agents can run autonomous multi‑step jobs, such as fixing code overnight or handling a full order flow, without constant human supervision [8].
story.origin: The pattern grew from the ReAct research (Reason + Act) published in 2022 by Princeton and Google, later called the agent loop in engineering blogs [1][4].

beforeAfter.how: Send the user query to an LLM once and return the generated text.
beforeAfter.breaks: Cannot handle tasks that need multiple steps or external actions; often incomplete or wrong.

beforeAfter.how: Ask the LLM to write out its reasoning before answering, but still a single call.
beforeAfter.breaks: Still lacks the ability to act on the world or observe results; loops are missing.

beforeAfter.how: Repeat: give context, let the LLM reason, call a tool, observe the tool’s output, feed back, and stop on a final answer or max steps [2][6].
beforeAfter.breaks: Requires careful stop conditions and engineering to avoid infinite loops.

production.title: Order troubleshooting
production.text: FoodieGo’s AI support agent receives a failed order report, calls the order‑lookup tool, sees the status, retries the payment, and confirms resolution, looping until success or timeout [2][6].

production.title: Menu recommendation refinement
production.text: The agent suggests dishes, calls a taste‑profile API, observes user feedback, and iterates the list until the user accepts a suggestion, all within the loop [7].

production.title: Night‑time code fix
production.text: An autonomous coding agent runs tests, observes failures, patches code, reruns tests, and stops when all tests pass, allowing work to continue after developers leave [8].

qa: Write test cases that the loop can call as actions.
Define stop conditions that prevent endless retries.
frontend: Expose tool endpoints (e.g., payment, recommendation) that the loop can invoke.
Show intermediate loop states to users for transparency.
backend: Implement tool APIs the loop will call.
Log each think‑act‑observe step for debugging.
leadership: Set limits on max steps and cost budgets for loops.
Monitor loop success metrics to decide product rollout.

items.what: Observability platform that records each LLM call and tool use.

items.what: Human‑in‑the‑loop review to catch bad loop outcomes.

atScale.lead: Demoing a loop is easy; running it for real users needs robust engineering around it.

ops.name: Latency
ops.text: Each iteration adds latency; need caching and parallelism.

ops.name: Cost
ops.text: Multiple LLM calls multiply token spend; enforce budgets.

ops.name: Reliability
ops.text: Handle tool failures and ensure loops can recover.

ops.name: Observability
ops.text: Log every step to debug loops in production.

ops.name: Safety
ops.text: Guardrails stop harmful actions before they happen.

ops.name: Scalability
ops.text: Distribute loop workers to handle many concurrent users.

atScale.takeaway: The model is only a small part; most effort is in building the surrounding loop infrastructure.

quest.oneLiner: Context management is picking and compressing the right facts for the model’s notebook so each call stays cheap and accurate.

story.pain: LLMs forget everything after each request, so developers either send the whole conversation or lose important details, leading to errors and high token costs.
story.idea: Treat the model as a stateless notebook and explicitly choose what facts, summaries, and recent messages to include – a practice called context engineering.
story.unlocked: Agents can stay coherent over many turns without blowing the token budget, and repeated prompts can be cached for speed.
story.origin: The term grew from early LLM prompt work and was formalized in blogs like LangChain’s “The rise of context engineering” [1] and Elastic’s discussion of context management for agentic workflows [2].

beforeAfter.how: Every turn is concatenated and sent to the model, hoping it remembers prior context.
beforeAfter.breaks: Token limits are hit quickly; latency rises; irrelevant old data dilutes the signal.

beforeAfter.how: Only the current user message is sent; the model starts fresh each time.
beforeAfter.breaks: The agent loses continuity; users must repeat information; experience feels broken.

beforeAfter.how: Store pinned facts (e.g., user’s address), keep a short summary of older turns, and send recent messages in full. Cache static prompt sections so they are reused without recomputation.
beforeAfter.breaks: Requires engineering to decide what to pin, how to summarize, and how to invalidate stale data.

production.title: Order status check
production.text: FoodieGo’s AI reads the user’s order ID (pinned fact) and a 2‑sentence summary of the last 5 interactions, then adds the latest question. This fits under the token limit and avoids re‑sending the whole order history [2].

production.title: Personalized restaurant recommendation
production.text: The agent pulls the user’s saved dietary preferences (pinned) and a compact summary of past likes, then adds the current query. Reusing the same preference block across calls is prompt‑cached, saving cost [1].

production.title: Support ticket escalation
production.text: When a complaint is filed, the AI includes the ticket ID (pinned), a brief summary of prior back‑and‑forth, and the latest user message. This ensures the model sees the whole case without exceeding the context window [3].

qa: Create test cases that verify pinned facts stay consistent across calls.
Check that summaries do not omit needed details.
frontend: Send only the latest user message plus a reference ID for the backend to fetch context.
Show loading indicators if context retrieval takes time.
backend: Implement a memory store for pinned facts and a summarizer for old turns.
Cache static prompt parts and invalidate them when the knowledge base changes.
leadership: Allocate budget for building the context store rather than buying larger models.
Measure cost per request before and after context compaction.

atScale.lead: A prototype works with a few dozen users; scaling to millions needs a robust context store, summarization pipeline, and caching layer.

ops.name: Latency

ops.name: Freshness

ops.text: Prompt‑caching cuts token usage by 30‑40% for static system prompts.

ops.name: Observability
ops.text: Track token budgets per request to avoid runaway costs.

atScale.takeaway: Most of the work is engineering the notebook – storing, summarizing, and caching – not the model itself.

quest.oneLiner: Guardrails are code that checks inputs and outputs around a LLM so the model can be tricked but the system stays safe.

story.pain: Developers let the LLM see user prompts directly, so attackers can inject hidden commands or leak data.
story.idea: Add a layer that validates every prompt, filters every response, and requires human approval for risky actions.
story.unlocked: The AI support agent can safely answer FoodieGo orders without exposing PII or executing unwanted commands.
story.origin: Guardrails were described as programmatic controls that sit around a model, validating inputs before the model sees them and filtering outputs before users do [3].

beforeAfter.how: Rely on the LLM to refuse unsafe requests on its own.
beforeAfter.breaks: Models can be fooled by prompt injection and still produce harmful output.

beforeAfter.how: Run a separate classifier after the model returns text and block bad results.
beforeAfter.breaks: The unsafe output may already have been sent to the user or cause side effects before it can be removed.

beforeAfter.how: Validate prompts, enforce least‑privilege tool use, run server‑side checks, require human‑in‑the‑loop for risky actions, and log everything.
beforeAfter.breaks: Adds latency and engineering complexity, but protects against prompt injection by assuming the model will be fooled [3][4].

production.title: Input validation
production.text: FoodieGo strips PII and rejects prompts that request illegal actions before they reach the LLM, using regex and rule‑based checks [3][15].

production.title: Output filtering
production.text: After the model replies, a safety filter removes toxic or off‑topic content and blocks instructions to order restricted items [4][18].

production.title: Human‑in‑the‑loop for orders over $200
production.text: If the LLM suggests a high‑value order, the system flags it and requires a supervisor to approve before the order is placed [5][9].

qa: Write test cases for prompt‑injection patterns.
Verify that logs capture rejected prompts.
frontend: Show users a clear error when a prompt is blocked.
Avoid sending raw user input directly to the API.
backend: Implement server‑side validation and audit logging.
Integrate human‑approval workflow for risky actions.
leadership: Allocate budget for guardrail tooling and monitoring.
Set policy that no LLM request bypasses validation.

items.name: Regex / rule engine
items.what: Fast check for disallowed words, PII patterns, and prohibited topics.

items.name: Guardrails AI library
items.what: Provides ready‑made input/output guards and structured validation [14].

items.name: Audit log service
items.what: Records each prompt, decision, and human approval for compliance.

items.name: LLM Guard (open source)
items.what: Runs runtime scanners for prompt injection and toxicity [12].

items.name: Approval dashboard
items.what: Shows flagged high‑value orders to a supervisor for manual review.

atScale.lead: A demo can turn on a single guardrail, but production needs validation, logging, and approval pipelines.

ops.name: Latency
ops.text: Each guardrail adds microseconds to milliseconds; balance safety vs response time.

ops.name: Observability
ops.text: Metrics and alerts for blocked prompts and human approvals.

ops.name: Compliance
ops.text: Retention of audit logs for regulatory audits.

ops.name: Fail‑over
ops.text: Graceful degradation if a guardrail service is unavailable.

ops.name: Scalability
ops.text: Deploy guardrails as stateless services behind a load balancer.

ops.name: Security
ops.text: Restrict who can modify guardrail rules.

atScale.takeaway: The model is only a small part; most effort is building, monitoring, and operating the surrounding safety code.

quest.oneLiner: Evals are repeatable tests that measure whether an AI agent meets the quality you need before you ship it.

story.pain: Teams built AI agents and only noticed problems after users saw bad replies, because they had no way to check relevance, tone, or safety at scale.
story.idea: Create an evaluation funnel: a golden dataset, code checks, and LLM‑as‑judge that runs automatically and acts as a release gate.
story.unlocked: You can catch regressions early, generate hypotheses, and ship with confidence that the agent behaves as expected.
story.origin: The evaluation funnel idea was described at Spotify as a way to put evals before experiments, not replace them [1].

beforeAfter.how: Humans read a few sample chats and mark them good or bad.
beforeAfter.breaks: Not scalable, slow, and misses rare failure modes.

beforeAfter.how: Use a third‑party leaderboard to pick the model with the highest overall score.
beforeAfter.breaks: Benchmarks measure generic abilities, not the specific success criteria of FoodieGo’s support agent.

beforeAfter.how: Run a golden test set, automated code checks, and an LLM‑as‑judge for tone, helpfulness, and safety; block release if thresholds fail.
beforeAfter.breaks: Requires engineering effort to integrate into CI/CD, but gives reliable, product‑specific signals.

production.title: Pre‑deployment gate
production.text: Before a new version of FoodieGo’s AI support agent is released, the CI pipeline runs evals on a curated set of user queries. If relevance or tone scores drop, the build is blocked [7][5].

production.title: Continuous monitoring
production.text: In production, a sample of live user requests is fed to the agent, the outputs are graded by an LLM‑as‑judge, and alerts fire when drift is detected [8][6].

production.title: Hypothesis generation
production.text: When evals flag a pattern (e.g., the agent often suggests unavailable restaurants), engineers create a targeted test and iterate quickly [1].

qa: Define the success criteria for relevance and tone.
Create the golden dataset of sample queries.
frontend: Expose a test endpoint for the UI to send sample chats to the eval runner.
Show eval results in a dashboard for quick feedback.
backend: Implement code checks that verify response formats and latency.
Integrate the LLM‑as‑judge into the CI pipeline.
leadership: Set the threshold scores that must be met before release.
Use eval trends to report AI health to stakeholders.

atScale.lead: Running evals in a demo is easy; making them reliable for millions of daily chats requires robust data pipelines and monitoring.

ops.text: Keep the golden dataset updated with new user intents.

ops.name: Latency
ops.text: Ensure eval runs add minimal delay to CI and live pipelines.

ops.name: Drift detection
ops.text: Alert when live eval scores move beyond set thresholds.

ops.name: Cost control
ops.text: Batch eval calls to limit LLM usage fees.

atScale.takeaway: The model is only a fraction of the work; most effort is in data, tooling, and ops that keep the evals trustworthy.
